annotationRationale: The integer restriction determines which fraction pairs are possible, and completeness requires a justified finite search. Reduction supports the primary grouping method, while listing distinct totals without repetition supports both routes.

classificationReview.areaRationale: The main subject is the integrality of rational sums, resolved using reduced denominators and integer restrictions. Number Theory better describes this than the current Prealgebra label.
classificationReview.areaCheck: Changing Prealgebra to Number Theory is justified by the central reduced-denominator and integrality restrictions.

review.questionCheck: All fourteen fractions (15−b)/b, for 1≤b≤14, must be considered, including unreduced forms and repeated choices. The achievable integer totals are {1,2,3,4,6,7,8,13,16,18,28}, giving 11 and agreeing with choice C. No stem, choice or figure contradiction is present.
review.alternativeMethodCheck: 2021_Fall_AMC_10B_Q07/group-reduced-fractions and 2021_Fall_AMC_10B_Q07/bounded-denominator-search are independently valid and both retained. They offer genuinely different completeness arguments: reduced-denominator grouping and a bounded integer search. The supplied fractional-part and reciprocal variants are covered by these routes.
review.annotationCheck: Integer restrictions and completeness appropriately form the assessed synthesis. Fraction reduction supports the grouping method, and roster notation supports counting distinct totals in both methods. Removing general unlike-denominator arithmetic from the direct mapping is justified.
review.areaCheck: Changing Prealgebra to Number Theory is justified by the central reduced-denominator and integrality restrictions.

methodReviews.mathCheck: The proof that an integer-sum partner has the same reduced denominator is valid. All fourteen fractions occur in the displayed groups. Integer pairs yield {4,6,8,16,18,28}; half-integer pairs yield {1,2,3,7,8,13}. The quarter pair adds only 3, and none of the six singleton groups has an integral double. The first two sets overlap only at 8, giving 6+6−1=11.
